chapter_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read (How I Taught My Grandmother to Read)
subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 50 minutes × 13 periods = 650 minutes
Total: 13 periods · 10h 50min

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
periods.activity_title: Activating Prior Knowledge — Literacy and the Elderly

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reflect and Respond (p.1): word web — why reading and writing matter
Reflect and Respond (p.1): four oral questions on elderly relatives and shared experiences

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the chapter title and asks students what they imagine when they hear it. Brief pair-share builds curiosity about the narrator and her grandmother.
Students complete the word web around the question of why reading and writing matter, individually first, then share across pairs. Teacher draws out responses on the board.

Open class discussion using Reflect and Respond oral questions: students share which languages their grandparents speak, how they spend time with elderly relatives, and what elderly family members enjoy watching younger people do.
Teacher briefly contextualises the story — north Karnataka village, weekly Karmaveera magazine, the novel Kashi Yatre — so students enter the text with a sense of setting.

periods.teacher_notes: This opening exchange surfaces students' existing connections to elderly relatives and regional languages, which the story calls on directly — Krishtakka's dependence on the narrator mirrors what students may have observed at home. Guide students away from one-word answers on the oral questions by pressing for a specific memory or moment. Tasks on word-building vocabulary (p.2) are not anchored here; flag them as self-study reading alongside the text.

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
periods.activity_title: Reading Aloud — The Village, Karmaveera, and Krishtakka

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reading for Meaning (p.2): vocabulary match — eight highlighted words to meanings

time_bands.activity: Teacher sets the reading context: students follow in their textbooks, track unfamiliar words, and note any moment that surprises them.

Teacher reads Part I of the prose aloud — from the opening to the narrator's return from the cousin's wedding — pausing at key moments (the midnight terrace scene, Krishtakka's tears) for students to visualise.

Students work in pairs on the vocabulary matching task in Reading for Meaning (p.2), matching highlighted words such as protagonist, episode, and concentration to their meanings, then verify answers as a class.

periods.teacher_notes: The prose moves between the narrator's affectionate tone and Krishtakka's quiet dignity — students should hear both during read-aloud. The eight vocabulary items in Reading for Meaning are all drawn from the passage students have just heard, so meaning can be guessed from context before the dictionary is used.

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
periods.activity_title: Cause and Effect — Mapping Krishtakka's World

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Check Your Understanding (p.6–7): cause-and-effect table — six entries from Part I

time_bands.activity: Teacher recaps Part I content through a quick oral quiz: why was Krishtakka in tears, what is Kashi Yatre about, and why did the narrator leave the village?
Students complete the cause-and-effect table from Check Your Understanding (p.6–7) in pairs, filling in causes for given effects and effects for given causes across all six entries.
Pairs share their answers; teacher facilitates discussion on any entries where answers differ, pointing back to the text as the arbiter.

Teacher poses the two bridging inference questions (tasks 4 and 5 in the summary): did the narrator expect tears, and how might she help? Students share one-sentence responses aloud — no written task.

periods.teacher_notes: The cause-and-effect structure in this section of the story reveals how Krishtakka's illiteracy creates a chain of consequences — poor transport, delayed magazines, the narrator's absence — that the task makes explicit. Tasks 4 and 5 (the narrator's expectations and how she might help) are treated as brief oral closure here; they are not anchored as written tasks to preserve the period's time budget.

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
periods.activity_title: Reading Aloud — The Resolution and Krishtakka's Triumph

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Check Your Understanding (p.9–10): six true/false statements on Part II

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces Part II: Krishtakka's declaration, Dassara as the deadline, and the reversal of the teacher–student hierarchy.

Teacher reads Part II aloud — from Krishtakka's bold resolution through the Dassara day scene and the gift of the published Kashi Yatre — with unhurried pacing at the grandmother's speech on determination.
Students individually answer the six true/false statements in Check Your Understanding (p.9–10), then discuss verdict and justification in pairs before a whole-class check.
Teacher draws attention to Krishtakka's line — 'For learning there is no age bar' — and asks students to hold that idea as they move toward extract-level analysis.

periods.teacher_notes: The true/false task on p.9–10 covers key plot facts and character values from Part II; students who have listened carefully during read-aloud will find it manageable. Watch for the common error of marking as false the statement about the narrator being the grandmother's first teacher — the text is explicit that the narrator taught Krishtakka the Kannada alphabet for the first time.

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
periods.activity_title: Extract Analysis — The Terrace Scene and Krishtakka's Tears

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Critical Reflection (p.10–11): Extract 1 — terrace scene, five analytical sub-questions

time_bands.activity: Students re-read Extract 1 silently (p.10–11), from Krishtakka's tears to the description of her affectionate hands touching the narrator's forehead.

Teacher leads close-reading discussion through all five sub-questions: the phrase 'never seen her cry in the most difficult situations', the mood-setting lines, the clue of rural custom, and which aspect is not emphasised in the extract.
Students write brief individual responses to the two analytical extract sub-questions (identifying rural setting clues; identifying lines that establish tender atmosphere) in their notebooks.
Two or three students read their responses aloud; teacher affirms textual grounding and redirects over-general answers back to specific lines.

periods.teacher_notes: This is the first extract-level close-reading in the chapter; students may tend toward plot summary rather than textual evidence. Press them to quote or paraphrase specific lines — the image of the open terrace, the midnight setting, and Krishtakka's silent response are the anchors for tender atmosphere. The MCQ and fill-in sub-questions are part of the same anchored task and must all be addressed.

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
periods.activity_title: Extract Analysis — Krishtakka's Declaration of Independence

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Critical Reflection (p.12): Extract 2 — grandmother's declaration, five sub-questions

homework.task_brief: Answer the following questions (p.12–13): attempt any two extended-answer questions on embarrassment, Kashi Yatre's significance, and the theme of determination

time_bands.activity: Students re-read Extract 2 silently (p.12): Krishtakka's 'I have decided I want to learn the Kannada alphabet' speech through the narrator's laughing reaction.

Teacher leads critical-reading discussion of all five sub-questions: what 'I want to be independent' reveals about character, the fill-in on age limits, why the narrator laughs, two qualities of the grandmother, and how the narrator makes assumptions.
Students write answers to sub-questions 3, 4, and 5 (SCR responses) individually in their notebooks.
Teacher previews the extended-answer questions (p.12–13) set as homework and clarifies what 'textual reason' means in that context.

periods.teacher_notes: Extract 2 is the pivot of the story — Krishtakka moves from helpless grief to determined agency. Students often read the narrator's laughter as unkindness; guide them to see it as age-based assumption, which the grandmother's quiet dignity then dismantles. The seven extended-answer questions (Answer the Following, p.12–13) go to homework; students are asked to attempt any two, keeping the load manageable.

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.13): binomial matching — eight pairs, then five original sentences
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.15): idiom matching — six learning idioms, then sentences

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes 'hide and seek' on the board and asks what type of expression it is, connecting to the text's use of the binomial.
Students match the eight binomials in Column 1 (sink or swim, on and off, etc.) with their meanings, using a dictionary where needed, then write five original sentences using their chosen binomials.

Students match the six learning idioms (to hit the books, to draw a blank, burn the midnight oil, etc.) with their meanings, then construct original sentences; pairs swap and check for correct use in context.
Quick whole-class share: one student reads a binomial sentence, another reads an idiom sentence; teacher corrects any usage issues on the spot.

periods.teacher_notes: Both tasks focus on fixed expressions — binomials and idioms — that appear in the story's language world. Stress that binomials have a fixed word order (sink or swim, never swim or sink) and that idioms are non-compositional (to draw a blank means to remember nothing, not to literally draw). Tasks on prefix formation (p.14) and on past-perfect tense (p.16) are reserved for the grammar-dedicated unit.

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
periods.activity_title: Prefixes and the Past Perfect Tense in Context

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.14): prefix formation — ten words with un/im/dis/in/mis/extra
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.16): simple past vs past perfect — five sentence fill-in tasks

homework.task_brief: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.16): paragraph cloze — ten blanks, simple past and past perfect

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws attention to 'unhappy', 'unusual', 'independent' from the story text, asking what each prefix contributes to meaning.
Students add prefixes (un, im, dis, in, mis, extra) to the ten words in Column 1 (p.14) and verify with a partner; teacher checks and discusses borderline cases such as 'disrespect' vs 'irrelevant'.

Teacher presents the grammar box on simple past vs past perfect using sentences from the story — 'Kashi Yatre which had been published' and 'my student had passed with flying colours' — to anchor the concept.
Students fill in the five sentence blanks (p.16) distinguishing simple past from past perfect, then compare answers with a partner before whole-class verification.
Teacher sets the paragraph cloze (p.16) as homework and advises students to identify the completed action before the other action in each clause.

periods.teacher_notes: Connect the past-perfect sentences directly to the story's timeline: Krishtakka 'had never been to Kashi' (past perfect — unrealised dream) precedes the narrator's arrival (simple past). Students commonly apply simple past to both clauses; the story examples give a memorable anchor. Task on identifying five words with prefixes from the story (task index 2) is left unanchored — encourage students to mark examples as they re-read.

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
periods.activity_title: Listening to a Talk on Digital Literacy

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Listen and Respond (p.17): digital literacy talk — five sentence-completion blanks (transcript p.259)

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the concept of digital literacy, connecting it to the chapter's theme: Krishtakka faced textual illiteracy; today's equivalent challenge is navigating digital information responsibly.
Students read the five incomplete sentences (p.17) before listening, predicting what kind of information will complete each blank.
Teacher reads the digital literacy transcript (p.259) aloud at a natural pace — one full reading — while students complete the sentence blanks with one to three exact words.
Teacher reads the transcript a second time at a slightly slower pace; students verify and correct their answers.

Whole-class answer check: students read their completions aloud; teacher confirms against the transcript and discusses why 'digital tools effectively and responsibly', 'personal data', and 'stay connected' are the key phrases.

Teacher draws a brief parallel: the transcript mentions the National Digital Literacy Mission as an institutional response to illiteracy, mirroring the story's individual response through Krishtakka and the narrator.

periods.teacher_notes: The transcript uses academic register and compound noun phrases ('digital transactions', 'cyber threats', 'IT training') that students may mishear; advise them to listen for the broad meaning first and fill exact words on the second reading. The connection between Krishtakka's textual dependence and the elderly citizens mentioned in the transcript — who need digital literacy to 'stay connected' — makes the thematic bridge natural and worth foregrounding.

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
periods.activity_title: Turncoat Debate — Learning Languages and Learning at Any Age

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Speaking Activity (p.17): turncoat solo debate — two topics, one minute each side

time_bands.activity: Teacher explains the turncoat format: the speaker argues 'for' for a fixed interval, then switches to 'against' for the same interval, using the sentence prompts in the textbook as scaffolding.

Students take four minutes to jot two 'for' and two 'against' points for whichever topic they choose — Topic 1 (learning a new language) or Topic 2 (learning happens only when young). Sentence prompts from p.17 are available.
Eight to ten volunteers deliver their turncoat debate, one minute per side; remaining students listen actively and note one strong argument from each speaker. Teacher times and prompts the switch.
Class votes on which side had the stronger argument for each topic, and teacher briefly surfaces how Krishtakka's story is evidence for or against Topic 2.

periods.teacher_notes: Topic 2 — 'Learning can happen only when you are young' — connects directly to Krishtakka's response to the narrator's laughter: 'For learning there is no age bar.' Students who choose Topic 2 will find the story a ready source of evidence for the 'against' side. Encourage students arguing 'for' to distinguish between ease of learning and possibility of learning — this keeps the debate intellectually honest.

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
periods.activity_title: Letter to the Editor — Students and Adult Literacy Campaigns

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Writing Task (p.17–18): formal letter to editor on student participation in adult literacy camps

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays the formal letter format on the board — name/address, date, subject line, salutation, three-paragraph body, complimentary close — and discusses how each element serves a different communicative purpose.

Students plan their letter in a quick outline: one sentence per paragraph capturing the main point — importance of student participation, benefits for students and society, and one concrete suggestion for spreading awareness.
Students write their full letter in formal register, incorporating specific arguments and a concrete suggestion; teacher circulates and provides formative feedback on register and clarity.
Paired peer response: each student reads their partner's letter and marks one strength (register, specific argument, or format) and one improvement point.
Two volunteers read their letters aloud; class identifies one formal register feature and one persuasive move in each.

periods.teacher_notes: Students should use formal salutation and complimentary close exactly as the format guide specifies; a common error is using 'Dear Sir or Madam' but closing with 'Yours sincerely' (appropriate only when the name is known) — the guide specifies 'Yours truly'. The writing task begins and ends in this unit: planning, drafting, peer response, and brief revision all happen within these fifty minutes.

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
periods.activity_title: India's Languages — Kinship Terms Across Five Tongues

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Learning Beyond the Text (p.21): kinship-terms table — six family roles in five Indian languages
Learning Beyond the Text (p.21–22): four literacy passages — NLMA, financial literacy, ELP, CCRT

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the 'Avva' footnote from the story — 'mother in north Karnataka Kannada' — and opens a whole-class question: what do you call your grandmother in your home language?

Students complete the kinship-terms table (p.21) — grandmother, grandfather, mother, father, sister, brother — across five Indian languages of their choice, consulting classmates who speak those languages and the Kannada column already filled.

Students read the four 'Do You Know?' informational passages (p.21–22) — on NLMA, financial literacy, the Early Literacy Project, and CCRT — individually, then share one fact they found most surprising.

Teacher draws connections between the literacy missions described in the passages and Krishtakka's private act of learning — individual determination and institutional support as two sides of the same goal.

periods.teacher_notes: The kinship-terms table works best when students with different language backgrounds fill in columns for each other — make this an oral exchange rather than silent individual research. The multilingual dimension of the table (Kannada is the anchor; students add their own languages) mirrors the story's celebration of regional literary culture. The gift-giving task (task index 2 in beyond_text) is left unanchored as a personal project students may pursue independently.
materials: Access to classmates as language sources

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
periods.activity_title: Whole-Chapter Synthesis — Literacy, Determination, and Intergenerational Bonds

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens a discussion on the chapter's central arc: how Krishtakka moves from illiteracy and dependence to literacy and agency. Students name the turning points — the midnight terrace, the declaration of independence, the Dassara deadline, the reversal of the feet-touching gesture.

Small groups of four discuss: 'What does the grandmother's act of touching the narrator's feet reveal about who holds real authority in the story — the older or the younger?' Groups nominate a spokesperson and prepare a two-sentence position with a textual reason.

Each group's spokesperson shares their position; teacher charts the responses — noting where groups agree that the act reverses hierarchy deliberately, and where they differ on whether the narrator is truly the authority or simply the medium.

Students write a paragraph — ten to twelve sentences — evaluating how effectively the story argues that education is a source of personal independence. They must name at least one specific scene and one specific line of dialogue as evidence.

Three volunteers read their paragraphs aloud; teacher highlights one example of effective textual grounding and one example of strong evaluative language from the readings, connecting them to the chapter's broader theme of intergenerational love and learning.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis draws on Krishtakka's journey as narrated by Sudha Murty — the serialised novel Kashi Yatre, the village setting, the Dassara deadline, and the published book as a gift — all of which anchor discussion in the story's specific world. The evaluative paragraph begins and ends within this unit; students do not continue or revise work from any earlier sitting. The digital literacy theme from the listening transcript and the multilingual kinship table from beyond-the-text can be briefly recalled as real-world extensions of the same literacy argument.

items.source_section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
items.source_lo: Student analyses character motivation, authorial purpose, and thematic significance using close reading of prose as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Krishtakka's tears, her declaration of independence, and the reversal of the feet-touching gesture.
items.item_stem: When the narrator returns from the cousin's wedding and finds Krishtakka in tears, she is struck by the sight because it is completely unprecedented. Which of the following best explains why Krishtakka's dependence on the narrator to read Kashi Yatre caused her such distress?

options.label: A
options.text: She was upset that the narrator had gone away without informing her in advance.

options.label: B
options.text: Her inability to read left her helpless and ashamed, stripping her of dignity despite the family's comfort.

options.label: C
options.text: She feared the narrator would not return and would miss the next episode of the novel.

options.label: D
options.text: She was angry that the magazine had arrived late and no one had brought it to her.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses cause of distress — the narrator's departure is not the core issue; illiteracy and helplessness are.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Misreads the grandmother's emotion as anxiety about the narrator rather than shame at her own dependence.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Focuses on the magazine's arrival rather than Krishtakka's inability to read it independently.

items.source_section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
items.source_lo: Student analyses character motivation, authorial purpose, and thematic significance using close reading of prose as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Krishtakka's tears, her declaration of independence, and the reversal of the feet-touching gesture.
items.item_stem:
Read the following passage and answer the questions below.

1. What does Krishtakka's act of touching the narrator's feet — a gesture ordinarily reserved for elders — reveal about the author's view of where real authority lies in the teacher–student relationship?
2. The story is narrated by a twelve-year-old girl, not by Krishtakka herself. Analyse how this choice of narrator shapes the reader's understanding of the grandmother's determination and dignity.
3. 'For a good cause if you are determined, you can overcome any obstacle.' Evaluate how effectively the story as a whole supports this statement, referring to at least two specific moments in the narrative.
items.visual_stimulus: Secretly, I bought Kashi Yatre which had been published as a novel by that time. I wrapped it in a silk cloth and gave it to my grandmother. She took the book in both hands and with great reverence touched it to her eyes. Slowly, she read out the title, then the name of the author and then the publisher's name and address. I knew, then, that my student had passed with flying colours.

expected_elements: The feet-touching reverses hierarchy; teacher role outranks age-based authority.
Child narrator highlights contrast between youth and Krishtakka's quiet, unassuming resolve.
Narrator's admiring tone guides the reader to see dignity where society might see embarrassment.
Two specific moments: midnight declaration and Dassara day reading of title and publisher.
Evaluation should acknowledge both theme and narrative craft, not just plot summary.

items.source_section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
items.source_lo: Student identifies key information and completes precise verbal recall tasks while listening to an informational talk.
items.source_context: A spoken explanation of digital literacy's three purposes and the Digital Saksharta Abhiyan.
items.item_stem:
Listen to the talk on digital literacy and decide whether each of the following statements is true or false. Write True or False next to each statement.
(1) Digital literacy today is limited to the ability to read and write printed text.
(2) One purpose of digital literacy is to help people recognise misinformation and cyber threats online.
(3) The Digital Saksharta Abhiyan was launched to provide IT training to people across India.
(4) Senior citizens are mentioned as one group that benefits from digital literacy by staying connected.

options.text: Digital literacy today is limited to the ability to read and write printed text.
One purpose of digital literacy is to help people recognise misinformation and cyber threats online.
The Digital Saksharta Abhiyan was launched to provide IT training to people across India.
Senior citizens are mentioned as one group that benefits from digital literacy by staying connected.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1 — False: digital literacy now extends well beyond reading and writing to include using digital tools, identifying reliable sources, and protecting personal data. 2 — True: the transcript explicitly names recognising misinformation, scams, and cyber threats. 3 — True: the transcript names the Digital Saksharta Abhiyan (DISHA) as a scheme to impart IT training across the country. 4 — True: the transcript states that digital literacy enables senior citizens to stay connected.

items.source_section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
items.source_lo: Student identifies key information and completes precise verbal recall tasks while listening to an informational talk.
items.source_context: A spoken explanation of digital literacy's three purposes and the Digital Saksharta Abhiyan.
items.item_stem: After listening to the digital literacy talk, answer the following question in two to three sentences: The speaker argues that digital literacy is essential for three distinct reasons. In your own words, state all three reasons and explain which one you find most persuasive for young people in India today, giving a reason for your choice.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The three reasons given are: (1) digital literacy empowers individuals — students, professionals, and senior citizens — to access and use information; (2) it promotes safe internet use by helping people recognise misinformation, scams, and cyber threats; and (3) it prepares everyone for a digital future where online services, job applications, and governance require these skills. Students may argue any of the three is most persuasive for young people, provided they give a textually grounded or personally reasoned justification.

items.source_section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
items.source_lo: Student argues for and against a position in a turncoat solo debate, switching sides with coherent reasoning.
items.source_context: Whether learning a new language is essential or whether learning is age-restricted.
items.item_stem: Describe, in about one minute of speaking, a specific moment from your own life or from a story you know where someone — young or old — successfully learned something new. What made that learning possible? Focus on narrating the moment clearly and explaining what it reveals about how learning happens.

expected_elements: Describes a specific, concrete learning moment — not a vague general statement.
Names what enabled the learning: motivation, support, determination, or opportunity.
Uses clear narrative sequencing — what happened, what changed, what followed.
Connects the moment to a broader insight about learning without being preachy.
Speaks audibly and fluently for approximately one minute.

items.source_section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
items.source_lo: Student argues for and against a position in a turncoat solo debate, switching sides with coherent reasoning.
items.source_context: Whether learning a new language is essential or whether learning is age-restricted.
items.item_stem: Conduct a turncoat debate on the following motion: 'It is never too late for anyone to learn something new.' Speak FOR the motion for one minute, then switch and speak AGAINST the motion for one minute. You must offer at least one specific reason with evidence or example on each side. You may draw on Krishtakka's story or any other example you find relevant.

expected_elements: FOR: at least one reasoned argument with an example — e.g. Krishtakka learning at sixty-two.
AGAINST: at least one reasoned counter-argument — cognitive decline, opportunity cost, or structural barriers.
Clear signposting of the switch between sides.
Arguments engage with evidence, not mere assertion.
Confident, audible delivery for both one-minute segments.

items.source_section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
items.source_lo: Student writes a formal letter to the editor making a persuasive case for a civic initiative, using appropriate register and structure.
items.source_context: A letter to a newspaper editor proposing a community reading-room for elderly residents in the neighbourhood.
items.item_stem: Your local area has many elderly residents who enjoy reading but have no accessible space to read or borrow books. Write a notice for the school notice board (in 60–80 words) informing students about a drive to collect old books and magazines for a neighbourhood reading-room for senior citizens. Include what is needed, how students can help, and a deadline.

expected_elements: Uses notice format: title, date, issuing body or name, and a clear heading.
States the purpose — collecting books and magazines for elderly neighbours.
Specifies a concrete action students can take and names a deadline.
Uses clear, concise language appropriate to a notice — no narrative padding.
Stays within the 60–80 word limit without sacrificing key information.

items.source_section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
items.source_lo: Student writes a formal letter to the editor making a persuasive case for a civic initiative, using appropriate register and structure.
items.source_context: A letter to a newspaper editor proposing a community reading-room for elderly residents in the neighbourhood.
items.item_stem: You have read about how access to reading material transformed Krishtakka's sense of dignity and independence. Write a formal letter (150–180 words) to the editor of a regional newspaper arguing that public libraries should extend their evening opening hours specifically for working adults and senior citizens who cannot visit during the day. Use a persuasive and formal register. Include at least two specific arguments and one concrete suggestion for how the library can make this work.

expected_elements: Follows formal letter format: address, date, subject line, salutation, body, complimentary close.
Opens with a clear statement of the problem — inaccessible library hours for working adults.
Presents at least two reasoned arguments: dignity of access, economic participation, or lifelong learning.
Includes one concrete, feasible suggestion — e.g. volunteer staffing or a two-evening-per-week pilot.
Maintains formal register throughout; no colloquialisms; closes with 'Yours truly' or 'Yours faithfully'.

items.item_stem:
The story of Krishtakka uses narrative sequences where one past event is completed before another begins. Rewrite each sentence below by selecting the correct verb form from the brackets, choosing between simple past and past perfect tense. Write your answers as full sentences.
(1) By the time Dassara arrived, Krishtakka ______ (learn / had learned) the entire Kannada alphabet.
(2) The narrator ______ (realise / had realised) her grandmother was in tears the moment she ______ (enter / entered) the house.
(3) Before the narrator ______ (give / gave) her the book, Krishtakka ______ (never read / had never read) a full Kannada novel on her own.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (1) By the time Dassara arrived, Krishtakka had learned the entire Kannada alphabet. (2) The narrator realised her grandmother was in tears the moment she entered the house. (3) Before the narrator gave her the book, Krishtakka had never read a full Kannada novel on her own.

items.source_lo: Student explores multilingual kinship vocabulary across Indian languages and connects institutional literacy programmes to real-world need.
items.source_context: Kinship terms in five Indian languages and four national literacy missions described in informational passages.
items.item_stem: The story opens with the Kannada word 'Avva', meaning 'mother' or 'grandmother' in north Karnataka. India's 22 scheduled languages carry distinct kinship vocabularies that reflect regional identity. Write the word for 'grandmother' in any three Indian languages other than Kannada and English. For each word, name the language it belongs to. Then, in one sentence, explain what having different words for 'grandmother' across India's languages suggests about the country's cultural diversity.

expected_elements: Names three Indian languages other than Kannada and English with the word for grandmother.
Each entry correctly pairs a language name with the kinship term used in it.
The one-sentence reflection goes beyond listing — it makes a point about diversity.
Response uses clear, complete sentences rather than bullet fragments.
Does not repeat Kannada ('Avva') as one of the three required languages.

items.item_stem: The informational passages in the chapter describe four national literacy initiatives: the National Literacy Mission Authority (NLMA), the National Centre for Financial Education (NCFE), the Early Literacy Project (ELP), and the Centre for Cultural Resources and Training (CCRT). Design a brief project plan (150–180 words) in which your school class takes up ONE of these four initiatives as a month-long awareness campaign. Your plan must name the initiative you chose, state who the target audience is, describe two specific activities your class will carry out, and explain how your campaign connects to the values in Krishtakka's story.

expected_elements: Names one of the four initiatives and correctly describes its target community.
Describes two distinct, feasible classroom or outreach activities.
Connects the campaign explicitly to literacy as dignity or self-determination from the story.
Project plan is structured — not a list of vague intentions — with a clear sequence.
Stays within 150–180 words without sacrificing any of the four required elements.
